title: The Overwhelming Allure of the Status Quo Bias
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article singles out the Status Quo Bias as, in the author's judgment, the most pervasive and underappreciated decision bias leaders face, even amid a well-known lineup of biases like confirmation bias, anchoring, and loss aversion. It defines the bias simply — people cling to familiarity and comfort, and default to continuing current practice even when outcomes are mediocre — and argues that this default is dangerous precisely because it's often the right call, which lowers vigilance against it. The recommended countermeasure is a recurring, deliberately neutral question: do we have good reasons for favoring the current state? If the case for the status quo isn't clearly strong, the piece argues leaders should treat that as a signal to change course.
points: The Status Quo Bias is singled out as the most pervasive and overlooked decision bias, ahead of more commonly discussed biases like confirmation bias and loss aversion.
The bias is defined as clinging to familiarity and comfort even against evidence that current practice isn't working — dangerous precisely because staying the course is often the correct call.
The bias is shown to specifically undermine strategic planning, dulling enthusiasm for new strategies in favor of the predictability of existing ones.
The recommended countermeasure is a recurring, neutral test: absent a clearly strong case for the current state, leaders should treat ambiguity as a signal to change course.
quotes: The prize for the most pervasive decision flaw likely belongs to the Bias of the Status Quo.
The Status Quo Bias can be summed up in two short sentences: People cling to familiarity, comfort, and certainty.
Maintaining the status quo is both natural and effective, unless what is in place isn't working.
The bias to maintain the status quo also gets in the way of strategic planning.
The solution to this challenge is to continually ask a simple question: Do we have good reasons for favoring the current state?
The natural inclination to stay the course is a confession about what we prefer.
